newsitem.title: KENYA: Rwanda's Kagame defends Congo on U.N. probe.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda's Kagame defends Congo on U.N. probe.

text.p: Rwandan strongman Major-General Paul Kagame defended on Wednesday Congolese President Laurent Kabila's conditions for a U.N. probe into reported massacres of Hutu refugees.

Kagame, Rwanda's vice-president and defence minister, told a news conference at the end of a six-hour visit to Kenya the probe had to be widened to cover a longer period than that envisaged by the United Nations and the team had to be neutral.

Kagame, whose rebels seized power in Rwanda in 1994, said civilians in the east of former Zaire were routinely slaughtered by Rwandan Hutu refugees and militiamen and this warranted a U.N. investigation.
"Kabila is demanding a wider scope of investigation into killings in the Kivu region before and after he took power. I do not see anything wrong in that," said Kagame.

"He also wants neutral people to be members of the team and not individuals who have already formulated opinions on the alleged killings and again I find nothing wrong with that. The United Nations is big enough to find other individuals," he said.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan is expected soon to name a new team to fly to Kinshasa to investigate the massacre reports after Kabila blocked an inquiry led by Roberto Garreton of Chile.

Kagame, whose forces helped propel Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni to power in 1986, admitted earlier this month that Rwanda planned and led the overthrow of President Mobutu Sese Seko in the former Zaire, now Democratic Republic of the Congo.
Kagame described his talks with Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi as "cordial and very fruitful" and said they had agreed to reopen the Rwandan embassy in the Kenyan capital Nairobi.
The embassy was closed down 13 months ago after a Rwandan diplomat was implicated in an attempted assassination of an exiled Rwandan Hutu politician, Kenyan officials said.

Kenyan police say the diplomat was arrested at the scene of an attack on former Rwandan interior minister Seth Sendashonga. Rwanda has accused Kenyan police of framing the diplomat, who was expelled from Kenya, and Moi of working against Kigali.
Sendashonga, a leading Hutu dissident now living in Kenya, was shot in the left arm and his nephew was critically wounded by three gunmen in the attack in June last year on the outskirts of Nairobi.
"The issue of the embassy was raised and it was agreed that it be reopened as soon as possible. I hope this can happen tomorrow or the day after," said Kagame.

He said the issue of leading Hutu residents in Kenya accused by Kigali of leading, taking part or planning Rwanda's 1994 genocide of an estimated 800,000 people would be dealt with in a broader context of the new ties between Rwanda and Kenya.
"We shall handle the issue of these people as we strengthen our bilateral relationship," he added.

Relations between Kenya and Rwanda have been frosty, especially over Nairobi's decision to allow the Hutus a safe haven. Moi was a close friend of late Rwandan Hutu president Major-General Juvenal Habyarimana.
Habyarimana's assassination in April 1994 sparked the genocide when loyal and angry supporters took up arms and hunted down Tutsis and Hutus opposed to his rule.
Political analysts said Kenya, undergoing a tense political period, had become increasingly uneasy with small but militarily powerful Rwanda's ties with leading Kenyan opposition figures.
Kenya's opposition is leading a campaign for constitutional reforms before a general election this year. They have warned Moi of a Zaire-style rebellion unless he gave in on reforms.
